name: McLean
distance_from_hq_phrase: 12 miles / ~22 minutes from our Fairfax Blvd office
geographic_anchor_paragraph: McLean, VA spans nearly 25 square miles of Northern Virginia's Potomac River corridor, split by the Capital Beltway into its estate-neighborhood eastern half and its Tysons-adjacent western half. Chain Bridge Road and Georgetown Pike are the corridors locals use to orient — Chain Bridge connects McLean to DC in 20 minutes, Georgetown Pike runs west toward Great Falls. McLean is 15 minutes from Vienna, 20 minutes from Fairfax, and sits closer to downtown DC than most Fairfax County communities.
audience_descriptor: Residential homeowners in McLean, VA and surrounding Northern Fairfax County neighborhoods including Langley, Chesterbrook, Franklin Park, Salona Village, and the Georgetown Pike corridor.

housing_patterns.title: 1950s-1970s ramblers, colonials & split-levels
housing_patterns.neighborhood_examples: Chesterbrook, Bryn Mawr, El Nido, Langley Forest (original homes), Franklin Park (original homes)
housing_patterns.context_paragraph: Built with 100-amp or early 200-amp panels and circuits sized for the appliances of the era — toaster, fridge, color TV, a window AC unit if you were lucky. Wiring is original cloth-insulated copper in the oldest homes, transitioning to thermoplastic in the 1960s. Some mid-1970s homes in McLean have aluminum branch wiring (NEC deprecated aluminum in 1972 but installation continued for several years). Plumbing is original galvanized steel running to copper at the fixtures. Insulation is thin — R-13 walls at best, often less. Fast-forward to 2026: induction range, central AC, two refrigerators, a tankless water heater, EV charger in the garage, and a home office running three monitors plus a printer. Modern load patterns overwhelm circuits the original builder never planned for.
housing_patterns.symptoms: Breakers tripping under modern loads on 100-amp panels never sized for today's appliances. Warm or discolored outlets from backstabbed connections in original wiring. Flickering lights when the HVAC cycles — often a loose neutral at the meter mast. Federal Pacific Electric (FPE) or Zinsco panels that fail to trip on overcurrent, a documented fire risk in 22101's unrenovated 1950s housing stock. Aluminum branch wiring (mid-1970s homes) with oxidized connections at outlets and switches.

housing_patterns.title: 1970s-1990s colonials, traditionals & custom estates
housing_patterns.neighborhood_examples: Georgetown Pike corridor, Wolf Trap-adjacent, Langley Forest (renovated), Hunter Mill-adjacent McLean parcels
housing_patterns.context_paragraph: 200-amp service is standard but many homes were wired with GFCI gaps in kitchens and bathrooms that predate the 1996 code requirement (NEC 1996 made GFCIs mandatory at every kitchen counter receptacle; pre-1996 builds usually have one or two if any). Estate-scale homes from this era often have detached structures — pool houses, guest cottages, workshops — with separate sub-panels that may not have been permitted or inspected. Plumbing is mostly copper with early PEX appearing in the 1990s. Central AC is standard. Many of these homes have been partially updated over the decades — a kitchen remodel here, a bathroom addition there — creating a patchwork of wiring vintages that can make troubleshooting complex.
housing_patterns.symptoms: GFCI gaps in kitchens and bathrooms — pre-1996 homes often have one GFCI or none where current code requires them at every counter receptacle. Intermittent faults from patchwork wiring vintages created by decades of partial remodels (a 1985 kitchen circuit spliced to a 1970s branch run). Unreliable sub-panels in detached pool houses, guest cottages, and workshops — many added without permits, with undersized feeders or incorrect grounding and bonding.

housing_patterns.title: 2000s-2020s teardown rebuilds, new construction & townhomes
housing_patterns.neighborhood_examples: Evans Farm, Tysons-edge (Spring Hill / Route 7 corridor), Langley Farms (new builds), Bryn Mawr (new builds), El Nido (new builds)
housing_patterns.context_paragraph: McLean's 2010-2019 construction wave (17.6% of housing stock) is the largest single-decade share — most of these are teardown/rebuild projects on lots originally built for 1950s-1960s ramblers. Newer homes are built to current code with 200-amp panels, AFCI protection on living-area circuits (NEC 2008+), and tamper-resistant outlets (NEC 2008). But newer homes aren't exempt from issues. AFCI breakers are sensitive by design and trip on noisy loads. Smart-home wiring done by a previous owner's contractor can leave neutral bonds incorrect. The service drop from Dominion may have been sized for the original 1960s rambler and not upgraded when a 6,000-square-foot replacement went up on the same lot — the panel is modern but the utility feed is undersized.
housing_patterns.symptoms: Nuisance AFCI breaker trips on vacuum cleaners, treadmills, and other motor-driven loads — the breaker is working as designed but the homeowner thinks the circuit is faulty. Smart-home wiring with incorrect neutral bonds causing phantom loads and intermittent switch failures. Undersized Dominion Energy service drops — the panel is 200-amp modern but the utility feed was sized for the 1960s rambler that previously occupied the lot, throttling the home's actual capacity.

troubleshooting.summary: Breaker trips repeatedly or won't reset
troubleshooting.body: A breaker that pops daily — or the moment you reset it — points to a short, an overloaded circuit, or a failed breaker. In McLean's 1950s-1970s homes (Chesterbrook, Bryn Mawr, El Nido), the original 100-amp panel may simply be overwhelmed by modern loads.

troubleshooting.summary: Outlets dead in one room but not others
troubleshooting.body: Usually a tripped GFCI you don't know about, a backstabbed connection that worked loose, or a wire nut that came apart in a junction box behind drywall. We trace the circuit map and find the break in 15-30 minutes.

troubleshooting.summary: Lights flicker when the AC or fridge kicks on
troubleshooting.body: Voltage drop from a loose neutral at the meter base or a damaged feeder. McLean's older neighborhoods with overhead Dominion service and heavy tree canopy are especially prone to service-entrance connection issues.

troubleshooting.summary: Burning smell or warm switch plates
troubleshooting.body: Stop using the circuit and call us. Almost always heat at a loose connection — and loose connections in walls cause fires. We find the heat source with an IR thermal camera and repair it before damage spreads.

troubleshooting.summary: Half the house has power, half doesn't
troubleshooting.body: An open neutral at the service entrance — a serious condition that damages electronics. We test the voltage on each leg of the panel and identify the failure point. Common after storms in McLean's tree-canopy neighborhoods.

troubleshooting.summary: AFCI breaker trips on normal appliances
troubleshooting.body: AFCI breakers in McLean's 2010s+ teardown rebuilds are sensitive by design and trip on noisy loads like vacuums and treadmills. We confirm whether the trip is nuisance or a real arc fault, and adjust the circuit accordingly.

light-fixture-installation.summary: Chandelier installation in a two-story foyer
light-fixture-installation.body: Heavy chandeliers in Langley and Georgetown Pike estates need structural ceiling support, a fan-rated or heavy-duty junction box, and safe high-access rigging. We assess the ceiling, install the right bracket, and wire the fixture to code.

light-fixture-installation.summary: Replacing builder-grade fixtures after a renovation
light-fixture-installation.body: McLean's teardown rebuilds often come with generic builder fixtures the new owner wants to upgrade. We swap them out and update the junction box and dimmer if needed.

light-fixture-installation.summary: Recessed lighting layout for a kitchen or living area
light-fixture-installation.body: Evenly spaced recessed lights transform a room. We cut the ceiling, install IC-rated housings, wire the layout, and connect a dimmer. Most 6-8 fixture layouts take half a day.

light-fixture-installation.summary: Outdoor sconce or landscape lighting installation
light-fixture-installation.body: Exterior fixtures need weatherproof boxes, GFCI protection, and outdoor-rated wiring. We install porch sconces, pathway bollards, and soffit lights that survive Northern Virginia weather.

light-fixture-installation.summary: Upgrading 1950s lighting in older McLean homes
light-fixture-installation.body: Original fixtures in Chesterbrook, Bryn Mawr, and El Nido homes often connect to cloth-insulated wiring and undersized junction boxes. We rewire the connection and bring the box up to current code before mounting the new fixture.

light-fixture-installation.summary: Installing a fixture you bought yourself
light-fixture-installation.body: You found it at Lamps Unlimited, Restoration Hardware, or online. We install customer-supplied fixtures of any brand and weight — just make sure it arrives with mounting hardware.

most_common_problem_paragraph.troubleshooting: Breaker trips on overloaded circuits. McLean's median home was built in 1982, but the 22101 ZIP (central and eastern McLean — Chesterbrook, Bryn Mawr, El Nido, Langley Forest) has housing stock from the 1950s with original 100-amp panels and circuits sized for a toaster and a window AC unit. Add an induction range, central AC, a home office, and an EV charger, and those circuits can't keep up. The second most common call is flickering lights — usually a loose neutral at the meter base or a voltage drop from an aging overhead Dominion Energy service connection.
most_common_problem_paragraph.light-fixture-installation: Chandelier installations in two-story foyers. McLean's estate homes — Langley Farms, Georgetown Pike, Franklin Park — have foyers and great rooms with 18- to 25-foot ceilings designed for statement chandeliers weighing 50 to 200-plus pounds. The junction box and ceiling structure must be rated for that weight, and the original builder didn't always plan for it. The second most common call is fixture upgrades in McLean's 1950s housing stock (Chesterbrook, Bryn Mawr, El Nido), where original wiring and junction boxes need to be brought up to current code before a modern fixture can go in safely.
